caption:
My job interview was on the way to the labour ward. No, really.

Fresh out of uni, after a degree that took five years instead of three. Double shifts, baby on the way, saving for a house.

A recruitment company called. I took the phone interview on the way to the hospital and didn't say a word.

Days after my daughter was born, I was sat in front of the panel. When I told them, they couldn't believe it. I got the job.

Character shows when it's inconvenient. That's the energy I bring to every client at JONRA.

caption:
Everyone was calling at 2pm. I was calling at 8pm.

My first summer in recruitment, everyone rang candidates while they were at work. Busy, distracted, 30 seconds before a no.

So I flipped it. In at 7am, still on the phone at 8 or 9pm, when people were home and actually had time to talk.

Same effort. Better timing. Much better conversations.

So here's my question for you: when does YOUR customer actually have time to talk?

caption:
“That's not what we agreed.” If you've ever heard those words, this one's for you.

In recruitment, I never placed anyone without the terms agreed first. The rate, the hours, and on temp-to-perm deals, exactly what happened at six months. No surprises, so nothing to argue about.

I bring that same thing to the businesses I work with now. Before any work starts, get three things in writing:
1. What's included, and what isn't
2. What it costs, and when it's paid
3. What happens if it changes

One page, signed by both sides, saves you a whole load of stress.

Save this one. And if you want your quotes and contracts tightened up, message me. Link in bio.

caption:
Your quote is your first impression. Is yours doing you any favours?

I'm all about efficiency, and quoting is where I see so many owners lose their evenings. Blank page every time. Retyping the same exclusions. Forgetting the payment terms.

Four things that make a quote work harder:
1. Break it down: labour, materials, timescales
2. Say what's not included
3. Put an expiry date on it
4. Follow it up within 48 hours

Then build it once as a template, and the next one takes minutes, not an evening.

You don't have to be the cheapest. You have to be the clearest, and the one who calls back.

Want a quote template built around how you work? Message me. Link in bio.

caption:
It took ten calls before some managers took me seriously. Ten!

In recruitment I knew that going in. So call one was just call one, and I used every call to learn something: how big the team was, who used agency staff, what they were spending.

Most quotes aren't lost on price. They're lost because nobody followed up. Try this:
Day 2: check they got it
Day 7: answer the question they haven't asked
Day 14: ask straight. Yes, no, or not yet?

A no today isn't a no next month.

caption:
You don't get Google reviews by hoping. Hoping is not a strategy.

In recruitment, we visited our staff on placement with uniforms, timesheets, lunch and fruit. Other agencies' staff told us theirs never visited, and asked to join us. Referrals were never a problem.

Reviews work the same way. Look after people properly, then make it easy for them to say so:
1. Ask at the right moment, when the job's done and they're happy
2. Make it one tap: a direct link or QR code
3. Put a review card in every order or invoice
4. Reply to every review

One of my clients, a home baker, now puts a review card in every order. Simple, and it works.

caption:
Thinking about your first hire? Come here, let's talk. This is my world.

Over ten years in recruitment, placing people and leading a team of my own. Here's what I'd sort first:
1. Know exactly what the job is
2. Write it down as a job description
3. Work out the full cost, not just the wage
4. Check they have the right to work in the UK
5. Plan their first week before they start
6. Decide how you'll measure a good job

Then look after them. When we placed nurses, we visited them on placement with uniforms, timesheets, lunch and fruit. People stay where they feel looked after.

Hire on purpose, not in a panic.

caption:
Is your business actually ready to grow? Be honest with yourself on this one.

In recruitment, before I tried to grow a client, I mapped everything: every team, who used agency staff, what they spent. Then I knew exactly where the next work was coming from.

Tick these off:
1. You know your numbers every month
2. Your prices cover your time, not just materials
3. Customers can find and contact you easily
4. Every enquiry gets followed up
5. Someone could run a day without you

Fewer than three ticks? Fix the base first. Growth on shaky foundations just makes the cracks bigger.

Small checks. Big difference. Motivation's temporary. Consistency is the key.

caption:
Motivation gets you started. It doesn't keep you going.

My son took up rugby years after everyone else. Not the biggest, not the fastest. He didn't wait to feel ready. He turned up, went in for every tackle and learned the game. A few years in, he was thriving. Proud dad moment, I'll be honest.

Myth: “I'll start when I feel ready.”
Truth: you feel ready after you start.

Myth: “Motivated people are disciplined.”
Truth: disciplined people don't wait for motivation.

Myth: “I'll be consistent when things calm down.”
Truth: things calm down when you're consistent.

Motivation's temporary. Consistency is the key.

caption:
Busy doesn't mean successful. I say this with love, because I've been there.

I'm all about efficiency, so when an owner tells me they're flat out, my first question is: how much of it is the same job, done again?

Myth: “I'm flat out, so I must be doing well.”
Truth: busy can mean underpriced.

Myth: “I'll sort the systems when it calms down.”
Truth: it calms down when you sort the systems.

Myth: “Nobody can do it like me.”
Truth: nobody can, until you show them how.

Work on the business, not just in it.
